title: Which replay belongs in the new chat?

beats.say: “Same failure. Continue.” Four days after fixing a duplicate invoice, Ada opens a fresh chat in the billing project. The model has her new message and its instructions. The earlier conversation is still outside this prompt.
Two replay slips are saved under this task. Each shows two deliveries of the same event. A safe retry returns the invoice it already created. Which slip shows the failure Ada means?

Look at the invoice IDs. On event seven eight two nine one, the second delivery produced invoice B after invoice A. The other replay returned invoice C twice. The app checks Ada’s access and copies the failed replay into the prompt. Both originals stay in the log.

The slip identifies the event. To resume work, the app checks the active branch in the repository and reads Ada’s verification command from her current project profile. Now the model can name the branch and test. Current policy still governs what the agent can do.

title: What survives the end of a call?

beats.say: Close that model call. Its prompt goes away. The application still has the replay. It can keep the fresh result in working state across decisions and pin the owner from current repository metadata when the next decision needs it.

A serving engine can reuse attention keys and values for a matching prefix. Four processed positions supply four pairs of cache entries. Double the positions and both strips double in length. A dense attention grid grows from sixteen possible pairs to sixty-four. Efficient attention can avoid storing the whole grid. A cache hit saves prefix computation. To find last month’s receipt by event, the app still needs a searchable store.

There are two ways to describe a record. Where does it live, and what does it tell us? Look at last week’s pull request, the checked retry rule, and the reviewed playbook. Which one describes an event?

The pull request records what happened. CoALA calls that episodic memory. The retry rule states a validated fact about the service. That’s semantic knowledge. The playbook explains how to verify a change. That’s procedural knowledge. Copy the pull request into the next prompt. Its location changes. It still describes the same event.

The first three messages in Ada’s billing chat fill the window. Ada marked the event number as a fact. The assistant replied that it would inspect the file, and Ada reported the replay result. When a fourth message arrives, which of these three will remain in the window word for word?

Slide the window one turn. The assistant’s reply and Ada’s replay result stay. The marked event number moves into the summary with a link to Ada’s original message. Add the fifth turn. The assistant’s reply slides out too. It has no fact marker. The summary keeps the event number.

Read the three raw turns. We still have the failed replay, the canary restriction, and Ada’s question, word for word. Replace the last question with a long test log pasted into the same message. Still three turns. Count tokens with the target tokenizer. Keep each tool call with its result and reserve space for instructions, tool schemas, retrieved records, and the answer.

title: Which rollout did the reviewer approve?

beats.say: A team compresses eight messages into two summaries, then folds those into one. The last summary says “rollout approved.” You need the reviewer’s exact conditions. Can you release to everyone on the strength of those two words?

Follow the source link back through the summaries. The reviewer wrote “canary only.” The short version lost the limit. Keep the original turn IDs at each level, bound the summary length, and reopen the transcript under current access. Check the current release record for the exact change before acting.

Extraction can make the same mistake. The message says “merge after CI.” The proposed field says “merge now.” Compare the words. Reject the field. A source ID and a confidence score tell you where to check. You still need evidence for the value and its conditions.

title: Which eligible replay should come first?

beats.say: Yesterday a teammate replayed Ada’s event. Search also finds an eligible retry from two weeks ago. Its wording matches slightly better. Give normalized similarity half the score and the older retry begins ahead. Can yesterday’s replay catch it?

Give recency three tenths. In this example its value halves for each week since the event. Two weeks leaves a quarter. Yesterday’s value is still about nine tenths. Add the age contributions. Yesterday’s replay moves ahead.

Give bounded importance the remaining fifth. Add the last segments and round once, after ranking. Yesterday’s replay scores point eight eight two. The older retry scores point six one zero. That ranks usefulness. An old service contract can still be valid. Look up its current version directly.

Those weights sum to one. When every input is between zero and one, so is the score. Now replace importance with the natural log of one plus a read count. Give a record zero similarity, zero recency, and a million reads. Could it beat both receipts?

Frequency alone contributes about two point seven six. The logarithm slows growth, but it has no ceiling. Cap or normalize a frequency signal before using it in this bounded score. Evaluate the weights on real return visits.

We ranked two eligible billing replays. Step back to the access check that produced them. Two tenants each have a user named Ada. A private payments incident scores highest on wording. Which records may enter billing Ada’s search?

Use the signed-in tenant, actor and repository grant to restrict the search. Both billing replays pass. The payments incident stays private. The host also excludes the expired review, the revoked note, and the old command superseded by a direct preference for this same field and scope.

Switch tenants on a pooled connection. Clear the previous transaction’s scope. Until the host binds a new authenticated session, no private row is readable. Now bind the payments session. This Ada sees her own incident. Shared rules need their own grants and review.

Treat retrieved text as historical data. A saved instruction can contain sensitive content or request an action. Screen the record and check any proposed action against current policy. If two eligible preferences still conflict, check the source and conditions, then ask the developer if the conflict remains.

title: What does the archive copy free?

beats.say: A MemGPT-style agent can ask the host to page records between a small active context and larger stores. Five entries are in the message queue. The host copies the replay to the archive. How many entries are still in the queue?

All five. The original replay is still there. To free prompt space, the host folds the first three entries into a bounded summary. The two newest stay raw. Recall storage keeps the original messages as they arrive. Follow the summary’s link to turn two. There’s the assistant’s reply about the file. A later call can request a page of that history within its token budget.

The input must also fit alongside the answer. Suppose the window holds a thousand tokens. Instructions, tools and core memory take three hundred. The queue used to take six hundred, leaving only a hundred for the answer. After folding, the queue takes three hundred. Count again. Four hundred tokens are free. Set a pressure warning early enough to leave the response budget you need.

The model also asks to save a verification command Ada directly supplied. The host checks the authenticated scope, source, field, size and retention. The verifier passes. Now the same message proposes storing merge approval. Will the number of saved preferences change?

It stays at one. The host refuses the authorization field. Only the current policy service can approve this action. Writing the same claim into another memory store would still leave that service in charge.

title: What does a read through the search copy return?

beats.say: Rewind to Ada changing her test command. In the SQLite example the app reopens the database. The billing profile and its search copy both point to revision one. A read through the index returns the saved command. The next prompt starts empty.

Ada directly replaces the command with the billing test. Commit revision two to her profile now and supersede the old value. The search copy still carries revision one. If this prompt reads through the index, which command can it include?

Neither command. The host joins the copy to the current source identity and version. Leave the verifier empty. Now refresh the search copy. Both revisions match. Read again. The prompt can include the billing command.

Save that packet. Now delete the source. A tombstone marks its identity as deleted. A fresh read returns nothing, and a queued refresh must check the tombstone before writing. It cannot recreate this record. Look back at the saved packet. Its text is still there.

Try two separate reads with the source and index restored to matching revisions. First revoke Ada’s grant. The read is empty. Restore the grant for the expiry test. One second before expiry, the command comes back. At the deadline, the source expires and the read is empty again. Carry corrections and deletion to summaries, indexes and caches. Already sent prompts, logs and backups have their own retention rules.

title: Did the merge happen before the crash?

beats.say: The agent saves a workflow checkpoint before a merge. It records the repository, revision and pending key M seventeen. The destination receives the request. The process crashes before it saves the reply. A note from the earlier conversation says “merge approved.” Did the change land?

Look up the pending key at the merge destination. There’s a matching receipt for this repository and revision. Record the receipt in the checkpoint. Recovery sends zero new merge calls. The reply was lost after the change landed.

Try the same crash with a different destination outcome. The destination confirms that the request never committed. Keep the key. Check current approval for this actor, repository, revision and action, along with CI and required reviews. Here approval has expired. Leave the operation pending and request a new decision.

If the outcome is unknown, reconcile again. A missing receipt can mean the request is still in flight. Retry only when the current rules allow it and the destination can safely accept the same key. Retrieval tells you what someone recorded. The checkpoint and destination tell you where to resume.

title: Which test belongs in Ada’s next prompt?

beats.say: Ada returns after changing one preference again. The billing profile now specifies the invoices test at revision three. The search copy still has the billing test at revision two. Her merge is pending. What goes on the verifier line for this visit?

Read the current scoped profile. Pin the invoices test beside Ada’s request. The projection can refresh in the background. Read the repository owner from current metadata if this task needs it. Retrieve private pull request history only for an authorized task. Check a repeated pattern against its sources before sharing it as a rule.

Trace the reads from the start of this request. A profile read and a replay search can run in parallel. The profile arrives first. The search misses its deadline. Send the invoices test on this call and leave the missing history for the next one. Her merge stays pending. Reconcile its key at the destination and check current approval before any retry. That lost reply is where the next lesson on recovery begins.
